paper_title: Calibrated Typed Decisions for Entity, Relation, and Event Extraction

sections.title: Abstract
sections.content: Information extraction models often perform well on the datasets they are trained on, but transferring to new domains and annotation guidelines remains challenging. Supporting user-specified types alone does not resolve this problem. We present CalOn, a unified 0.6B-parameter encoder for entity, relation, and event extraction across datasets and schemas. The model jointly encodes text and type definitions, then directly identifies entity spans, relations between spans, and event triggers and arguments. Its extraction decisions consider the requested types together, using their combined evidence to identify relevant candidates before assigning a type. This gives all three tasks a common probabilistic formulation while keeping every extracted mention anchored to the input text. We train on diverse sources, and supplement supervised learning with a reward that encourages correct extractions and penalises incorrect ones. Across 40 benchmarks, CalOn outperforms the evaluated baselines on most benchmarks. It leads all reported relation extraction benchmarks and achieves the highest average F1 for event triggers and arguments with gold triggers. The same model also performs strongly on aspect sentiment triplet extraction and pronoun resolution through its span-pair formulation. A correction for the probability bias introduced during training improves confidence estimates for entities, relations, and event arguments after calibration, with little change in F1.

sections.title: Introduction
sections.content: Information extraction (IE) converts plain text into structured records of entities, relations, and events. The required information varies across applications, so an extractor must follow schema specifying the types to identify. For example, job-description analysis requires identifying skills, qualifications, and experience (Green et al., 2022). Traditional The corresponding author is Chenghua Lin, who can be contacted at chenghua.lin@manchester.ac.uk. 1 systems are trained for fixed set of types, while recent models accept type names, descriptions, or annotation guidelines as part of the input (Sainz et al., 2024; Zaratiana et al., 2025). This allows users to specify what to extract without training separate model for every schema. The field has therefore moved towards general-purpose extraction, with single model intended to serve multiple tasks and datasets (Lu et al., 2022a; Wang et al., 2023). Supporting new schema does not by itself ensure accurate extraction on new dataset. Models must transfer beyond the domains and annotation conventions represented in their training data (Bassignana and Plank, 2022; Sainz et al., 2024). Discriminative models predict spans and their types directly from the input. UniEX (Ping et al., 2023), GLiNER (Zaratiana et al., 2024), GLiNER2 (Zaratiana et al., 2025), and GLiFormer (Knowledgator Team, 2026) support flexible their performance varies across schemas, but domains and extraction tasks, as our evaluation shows. Generative models such as UIE (Lu et al., 2022b), InstructUIE (Wang et al., 2023), and GoLLIE (Sainz et al., 2024) express extraction targets through text generation. This accommodates detailed instructions, but generated outputs can introduce unsupported entities or fail to preserve the original mention boundaries. GPT-NER reports false entity predictions (Wang et al., 2025), while GNER documents boundary errors and omissions, additions, or changes to input words (Ding et al., 2024). The remaining challenge is to support userspecified schemas while maintaining extraction accuracy across domains and annotation guidelines. To address this challenge, we investigate whether reward-based training can improve schema-conditioned extractor beyond likelihood supervision alone. We present CALON, unified 0.6B-parameter encoder for entity, relation, and event extraction. Drawing on RLCDs emphasis on decisions with explicit probabilities (TypeSafe AI, 2026), we supplement supervised learning with optimisation of sampled extraction decisions. As in GRPO (Shao et al., 2024), multiple predictions for the same input provide reward baseline without requiring an additional critic. For each candidate span or span pair, we sample predictions by adding Gaussian noise to the type scores. Correctly typed extractions receive positive rewards, false positives and incorrect types receive negative rewards, and predictions of no extraction receive zero reward. We compare each predictions reward with the average reward of the other samples and use this difference to reinforce higher-reward decisions. The resulting objective combines likelihood supervision with direct optimisation of the expected reward of sampled extractions. The motivation is to strengthen correct predictions when the model can also produce incorrect alternatives. For the same candidate, changing the type scores can lead to correct extraction, wrong type, or false positive. Comparing their rewards gives an additional training signal that favours the correct extraction over these mistakes. We use this signal to supplement likelihood supervision, aiming to make the model less likely to return an incorrect prediction when its scores change. Across 40 benchmarks, CALON outperforms the evaluated baselines on most benchmarks. It leads every reported relation extraction benchmark, including tasks represented as span-pair extraction such as aspect sentiment triplet extraction, pronoun resolution, coreference, and temporal and causal relations between events. It also achieves the highest average F1 for event triggers and arguments with gold triggers. These results demonstrate that single extraction model can transfer across datasets and support tasks beyond conventional entity, relation, and event extraction. We make the following contributions. 1. We introduce CALON, unified encoder for extraction under user-specified schemas. It handles entities, relations, and events through predictions over spans and span pairs. The same formulation also supports tasks beyond conventional IE (3). 2. We develop training objective that combines likelihood supervision with relative rewards on sampled extraction decisions. Gaussian perturbations generate predictions for each candidate, and comparison of their rewards guides the model towards correct extractions over false positives and incorrect type assignments, without an additional critic (3.3).

sections.title: 2 Related Work
sections.content: Extraction across schemas and data sources. UIE (Lu et al., 2022b) unifies entity, relation, and event extraction through structured generation, while USM (Lou et al., 2023) and UniEX (Ping et al., 2023) use schema-guided matching. InstructUIE (Wang et al., 2023) uses instruction tuning, and GoLLIE (Sainz et al., 2024) incorporates annotation guidelines to support generative extraction under user-specified schemas. GLiNER (Zaratiana et al., 2024) and GLiREL (Boylan et al., 2025) match spans and span pairs, respectively, to requested types. GLiNER2 (Zaratiana et al., 2025) and GLiFormer (Knowledgator Team, 2026) support multiple tasks within one model. Training resources have also expanded through LLM annotations and synthetic examples, as in UniversalNER (Zhou et al., 2024), FiNERweb (Golde et al., 2026), and GUIDEX (Fuente et al., 2025). Combining sources requires handling differences in annotation coverage, since an unlabelled span is not necessarily negative example (Jie et al., 2019; Li et al., 2021). Learning extraction decisions. Span-based IE models use null class to reject non-entity spans (Eberts and Ulges, 2020; Zhong and Chen, 2021). For generative IE, LA-RL (You et al., 2026) applies reinforcement learning through label-aware selfreflection. Inspired by RLCD (TypeSafe AI, 2026), CALON adds reward term for sampled span and span-pair predictions. Correctly typed extractions receive positive rewards, while false positives and incorrect type assignments receive negative rewards. Calibration. Temperature scaling can improve the calibration of neural-network predictions after training (Guo et al., 2017). Calibration can also be improved through training, with label smoothing helping pre-trained Transformers on out-of-domain data (Desai and Durrett, 2020). Even when probabilities are calibrated, selecting threshold to maximise F1 remains dependent on the distribution of prediction scores, as shown for binary classification by Lipton et al. (2014). Class-dependent sampling can introduce separate bias in probability estimates. Corrections for this effect have been studied in rare-event logistic regression (King and Zeng, 2001) and click prediction (He et al., 2014). CALON applies this correction principle to the lower loss weight assigned to null candidates in span and span-pair extraction. 2 Figure 1: Overview of CALON: (a) schema-text encoding with type-candidate interaction and bilinear scoring over the queried types and null class, and (b) the RLCD reward on sampled typed decisions added to the supervised loss.

sections.title: 4 Experimental Setting
sections.content: Training data. We train on 3.1M instances from 84 sources covering entities, relations, and events: human-labelled data, LLM-annotated text, and synthetic examples spanning diverse domains, genres, and schemas. We check synthetic annotations with additional models, remove near-duplicate texts, and filter training texts that substantially overlap with evaluation sentences. The training-data generation pipeline does not use evaluation-set texts or annotations as inputs, demonstrations, or style references. No labelled examples from any target dataset are used for training, model selection, or calibration. Appendices B.1 and describe the preparation, sampling, type distribution and domain coverage. Evaluation. We evaluate on 40 benchmarks covering NER, RE, and EE across multiple domains. Appendix B.2 describes the datasets and scoring. We report exact-match micro F1 for each benchmark. Each benchmark receives equal weight when computing average F1. The main results use type descriptions for models that support them. Appendix reports results with type names alone. Directed relation predictions must also match the gold direction. For RE, we report end-to-end F1 and F1 with gold entity spans. For EE, we report trigger classification F1 and argument classification F1 with gold and predicted triggers. Baselines. We compare with GLiNER2-large (Zaratiana et al., 2025), GLiFormer-large (Knowledgator Team, 2026), GNER-LLaMA-7B (Ding et al., 2024) (NER only), InstructUIE (Wang et al., 2023), and GoLLIE-7B (Sainz et al., 2024), and for RE with gold entities GLiREL-large (Boylan et al., 2025), with default decoding and the same scoring code. GLiFormer, GNER, InstructUIE and GLiREL receive type names only, following their released interfaces; adding descriptions led to invalid outputs for GNER and InstructUIE. For RE with gold entities, we match the other baselines end-to-end relation endpoints to gold entities by span or mention text and discard unmatched relations. GLiREL receives gold entities directly (Appendix B.3). Implementation. We use Qwen3-0.6B (Qwen Team, 2025) as our backbone to limit the computational cost of training and inference. We remove its causal mask so that text and schema tokens can attend to the full input (Li et al., 2023). We select the checkpoint, hyper-parameters, temperature, and extraction thresholds using only validation data from the training sources. Appendix B.4 provides further details.

sections.title: 5.1 Main Results
sections.content: Entity extraction. CALON achieves the highest average F1 on CrossNER, specialised entity extraction, and personal information extraction  (Table 1)  . Its largest gains are on scientific, biomedical, and measurement text. GLiFormer leads on CrossNER Music and Science, while InstructUIE leads on MIT Restaurant. InstructUIEs Restaurant score raises its MIT average above CALONs, and both MIT datasets were included in training for the evaluated InstructUIE checkpoint (Appendix B.3). Relation extraction. CALON leads every reported RE benchmark, both with gold entities and where end-to-end scoring is available  (Table 2)  . The same span-pair formulation also performs well on ASTE and pronoun resolution. End-to-end results are omitted for datasets that annotate relations only for selected entity pairs. GLiREL is evaluated only with gold entities because it does not support end-to-end extraction. We also compare GLiREL under two candidate-pair settings (Appendix B.3). When only pairs with an annotated relation are supplied, its average relation typing accuracy across the 18 RE benchmarks is 40%, compared with 79% for CALON. When every pair of gold entities is considered, their average F1 scores are 2.6 and 49.8, respectively. The latter setting tests both relation typing and rejection of unrelated pairs, highlighting an important requirement for relation extraction. Event extraction. CALON achieves the highest average F1 for trigger classification and argument classification with gold triggers  (Table 3)  . InstructUIEs CASIE score raises its average end-to-end argument F1 above CALONs. The CASIE training split was included in training for the evaluated InstructUIE checkpoint (Appendix B.3). Excluding CASIE, CALON achieves the highest average F1 for all three EE metrics, with end-to-end argument F1 of 10.9 compared with InstructUIEs 8.4. Individual dataset exceptions, including M2E2 and SPEED++ zika, are discussed in Appendix C.

sections.title: 5.4 Calibration
sections.content: Null-class correction addresses the probability bias introduced by giving null candidates less weight in the training loss. After correction and refitting, average expected calibration error falls from 0.25 to 0.10 for relations, from 0.33 to 0.23 for entities, and from 0.51 to 0.39 for event arguments, with little change in F1  (Table 9)  . The results indicate more accurate confidence estimates with similar extraction accuracy. Event predictions reuse the entity and relation calibration parameters. Their calibration also improves, although event arguments retain the highest average calibration error.

sections.title: 5.5 Efficiency
sections.content: For given schema, CALON scores all queried types and candidates in one forward pass. Under the same PyTorch setting, it processes 120 sentences per second, 5 to 25 times the throughput of the baselines (Table 4, Appendix G). This advantage includes GLiNER2 and GLiFormer, which have similar parameter counts. CALON also achieves the highest average NER F1 among the compared models. Its peak GPU memory usage is 8.0 GB, higher than GLiNER2 and GLiFormer, so the throughput advantage is accompanied by greater runtime memory use. sections.title: 6 Conclusion
sections.content: We presented CALON, unified 0.6B-parameter encoder for extraction under user-specified schemas. The model handles entities, relations, and events through span and span-pair predictions. Its training objective combines likelihood supervision with relative rewards on sampled extractions, favouring correct predictions over false positives and incorrect type assignments. Across 40 benchmarks, CALON outperforms the evaluated baselines on most benchmarks and leads every reported relation extraction benchmark. It also achieves the highest average F1 for event triggers and arguments with gold triggers. Its advantages extend to tasks represented as span-pair extraction, including aspect sentiment triplet extraction, pronoun resolution, coreference, and temporal and causal relations between events. Probability correction and calibration improve confidence estimates across all three extraction tasks with little change in F1.

sections.title: Limitations
sections.content: Our training data and evaluation are limited to English, and transfer to other languages has not been tested. Candidate spans are capped at 32 tokens, and relations are predicted only between spans within the same input. These limits leave longer mentions and relations across inputs outside the models current scope. Much of the training data is annotated by LLMs. Voting across annotators and checks by judges help reduce shared biases but cannot fully eliminate them. Calibration parameters are fitted on validation data from the training sources, and the resulting probabilities may remain imperfect when the domain changes. We report results from single seed because repeating training and the full evaluation across 40 benchmarks would require substantial additional computation.

sections.title: Ethical Considerations
sections.content: When applied to text containing personal information, extraction systems can make sensitive details easier to identify and aggregate. Such applications should respect privacy and the conditions under which the data were obtained. LLM annotations may also retain shared biases despite our annotation Predictions and confidence estimates checks. should be reviewed before they are used in decisions that affect individuals.

sections.title: B Additional Experimental Details
sections.content: B.1 Data Preparation and Sampling Sources and schemas. Human-labelled sources include Few-NERD with fine-grained entity types (Ding et al., 2021), MASSIVE with slot annotations (FitzGerald et al., 2023), and the event datasets MAVEN-Arg (Wang et al., 2024), GENEVA (Parekh et al., 2023), RAMS (Ebner et al., 2020), and PHEE (Sun et al., 2022). FiNERWeb (Golde et al., 2026) provides LLM-annotated web passages, and Pile-NER (Zhou et al., 2024) provides LLM annotations of texts sampled from the Pile. We use Qwen3.8-27B to generate additional texts and annotations. These sources include new annotations of REBEL texts (Huguet Cabot and Navigli, 2021) and CC-News articles1, as well as synthetic texts generated from combinations of genres, domains, and schemas. Table 13 lists the genres and domains, and Figure 5 gives the generation prompts. Checking generated annotations. For most generated or reannotated sources, Nemotron-3Nano-Omni-30B-A3B (NVIDIA et al., 2026) independently annotates each text. When its annotations differ from those of Qwen3.8-27B, gpt-oss-120b (OpenAI, 2025) resolves the disagreements. For subset of synthetic sources, four additional models annotate each text independently of the generator. These are gpt-oss-120b, Nemotron, Phi-4 (Abdin et al., 2024), and Mistral-Small-24B (Mistral AI, 2025). Together with the generator, they provide five annotations. candidate mention, relation, trigger, or argument is accepted when majority of the models that provide an annotation agree on it. This requires three votes when all five models participate. Remaining disagreements 1https://commoncrawl.org/blog/news-dataset-a vailable are accepted or rejected only when both judges, gpt-oss-120b and Qwen3.8-27B, agree. If disagreement remains unresolved, or no model provides an annotation for type, we remove that type from the queried schema for the text. Retained types therefore have known annotation status. Duplicate removal and incomplete annotations. Within each synthetic source, we remove nearduplicate texts using all-mpnet-base-v2 embeddings and cosine similarity threshold of 0.9. We also compare training texts with evaluation sentences using word 5-grams. training text is removed when their overlap covers at least 80% of the 5-grams in either text. RAMS and GENEVA annotate only some events in each passage. For these sources, event types and argument roles without an annotated occurrence are marked unknown rather than absent. Sampling. We sample with replacement from pool of 3.1M training instances. With 40,000 updates and global batch size of 128, the sampling budget is 5.12M draws, including repeated samples. UniMax (Chung et al., 2023) distributes this budget as evenly as possible across sources. The allocation for each source is capped at four times its number of training instances. The resulting sampling proportions are approximately 35% entity, 41% relation, and 23% event examples. B.2 Evaluation Datasets and Scoring Entity extraction. The NER evaluation covers the five CrossNER domains of AI, literature, music, politics, and science (Liu et al., 2021), as well as MIT Movie and MIT Restaurant (Liu et al., 2013). It also includes SciERs in-domain and out-of-domain test sets (Zhang et al., 2024), GENTLE (Aoyama et al., 2023), BioRED (Luo et al., 2022), and MeasEval (Harper et al., 2021). Personal information extraction is evaluated on ai4privacy (Ai4Privacy, 2025) and the legal and medical subsets of spy (Savkin et al., 2025). Table 11 lists the domains, type counts, and evaluation sizes. Each input is queried with the datasets full entity schema. queried type with no gold mention is treated as absent for scoring. We split spy documents into chunks of at most 1,200 characters, with boundaries at whitespace outside entity spans. Relation extraction. We evaluate on the six CrossRE domains (Bassignana and Plank, 2022), using the relation definitions from the paper as descriptions. Other RE datasets are SciER, 13 BioRED, MeasEval, and Re-TACRED (Stoica et al., 2021). We also represent four ASTE datasets (Xu et al., 2020) as directed relations from aspect spans to opinion spans, with sentiment as the relation type. Additional tasks are converted to span-pair extraction. In GAP (Webster et al., 2018), relation links the designated pronoun to coreferent person In LitBank (Bamman et al., 2020), each name. mention is linked to the nearest preceding mention of the same entity within the input. We use all LitBank documents for evaluation. In MAVEN-ERE (Wang et al., 2022), relation candidates are event and time-expression mentions. Temporal, causal, and subevent links use representative mentions of each event within the input. Event coreference links later mentions to the first mention of the same event. We report only the gold-entity setting for BioRED, GAP, LitBank, MAVEN-ERE, and Re-TACRED. Their converted evaluation inputs use representative concept mentions, designated mentions, or supplied event and coreference mentions. End-to-end extraction is not evaluated under these conversions. Long inputs are divided into chunks outside annotated spans, and links whose endpoints fall in different chunks are excluded for every model. The converted LitBank and MAVEN-ERE scores therefore measure span-pair extraction within an input rather than the original document-level task. Event extraction. We evaluate on CASIE (Satyapanich et al., 2020), MLEE (Pyysalo et al., 2012), M2E2 (Li et al., 2020), MAILEX (Srivastava et al., 2023), SENTiVENT (Jacobs and Hoste, 2022), and SPEED++ (Parekh et al., 2024). For SPEED++, we use the released English files en-mpox.json and en-zika.json and retain mpox and zika as their benchmark labels. We report trigger classification and argument classification with both gold and predicted triggers. Scoring. We compute exact-match micro F1 for each benchmark and give each benchmark equal weight in averages. An entity prediction must match both the character offsets and the type of gold mention. relation prediction must match the two spans and the relation type. Directed relations must also match the direction. BioRED relations are symmetric, so reversed endpoints are treated as equivalent. An event argument must match the trigger span and event type, the argument span, and the argument role. We also measure the false-positive rate on absent types and the miss rate. The former is the fraction of type queries with no gold occurrence for which the model returns at least one prediction. The latter is the fraction of gold mentions without an exact matching prediction. B.3 Evaluation Adaptations Input formats. GNER (Ding et al., 2024) was trained on Pile-NER (Zhou et al., 2024). Following its input format, we split texts into words and separate punctuation into individual tokens. For GoLLIE (Sainz et al., 2024), each type is defined as Python class with its description in the docstring. We leave docstrings empty when evaluating without descriptions and provide no examples in either setting. GLiNER2 (Zaratiana et al., 2025) is evaluated on events through its structured extraction interface. Relations with gold entities. CALON and GLiREL receive gold entity spans directly. For the other baselines, we match the endpoints of their end-to-end relation predictions to gold entities. We first use an exact span match. If none exists, we use the nearest gold mention with the same text, ignoring case. Relations with an unmatched endpoint are discarded. These adapted scores still depend on the baselines identifying the mentions and do not isolate relation prediction in the same way as supplying gold entities directly. Arguments with gold triggers. For GLiNER2 and GoLLIE, we align predicted events with gold triggers of the same event type and retain the arguments of matched events. match is accepted when the trigger spans are identical, the predicted span contains the gold span, or their trigger texts are identical. InstructUIE predicts arguments for an event type rather than for an individual trigger. We provide the gold event types and assign each predicted argument to the nearest gold trigger of that type. GLiREL. We split texts into words and punctuation, with additional token boundaries at the start and end of every gold entity. GLiREL receives these entities and the relation type names, with hyphens and underscores replaced by spaces. It scores every ordered pair of gold entities, and we retain the highest-scoring type when its score passes the extraction threshold. Predictions assigned the no relation label are not returned as relations. We select the threshold on the REBEL calibration split from {0.05, 0.1, 0.2, ... , 0.9}. On the same split, we compare queries with and without an additional no relation label. We retain this label 14 because it gives higher F1, 18.1 compared with 17.2, and select threshold of 0.05. The evaluated configuration therefore includes both threshold and label for rejecting pairs. We separately measure relation typing when only pairs with gold relation are supplied. Across the 18 RE benchmarks, GLiRELs mean typing accuracy is 40.0%, compared with 79.0% for CALON when taking its most probable non-null type. With all ordered pairs of gold entities as candidates, their average F1 scores are 2.6 and 49.8. These metrics answer different questions. The first measures typing on positive pairs, while the second also requires rejecting unrelated pairs. GLiRELs low F1 in the latter setting is associated with low precision. Its 100% typing accuracy on GAP and LitBank is expected because each has only one relation type. Training coverage. The released training configuration associated with the evaluated InstructUIE checkpoint includes MIT Movie, MIT Restaurant, and CASIE2. GoLLIEs training includes TACRED and ACE05 (Sainz et al., 2024). Re-TACRED revises labels for TACRED sentences (Stoica et al., 2021), while M2E2 uses the ACE event types. These are different forms of prior exposure. The former involves shared source sentences, whereas the latter involves shared event types. We mark the relevant MIT, CASIE, and Re-TACRED scores with . Such exposure is relevant to interpreting the results, but the comparison does not isolate its effect from other differences between models. B.4 Architecture and Training Settings Architecture and candidate limits. We use bfloat16 mixed precision. Candidate spans contain at most = 32 tokens. Input texts contain at most 1,024 tokens, and the combined text and schema contain at most 3,072 tokens. The projection dimension is = 256, and width embeddings have dimension 32. We use = 2 interaction blocks with four attention heads each, feed-forward dimension of 4A, GELU activation (Hendrycks and Gimpel, 2023), and dropout of 0.1. The bilinear scoring dimension is = 64. Relation candidates are formed from at most 24 entity spans per instance. Optimisation. We train with AdamW optimiser (Loshchilov and Hutter, 2019). The learning rate is 4 105 for the encoder and 2 104 for 2https://github.com/BeyonderXX/InstructUIE/bl ob/master/configs/multi_task_configs/train_tasks .json the prediction heads. Weight decay is 0.01, and gradients are clipped at 1.0. The schedule uses 10% warm-up followed by linear decay. Training runs for 40,000 updates on 32 GPUs with global batch size of 128, or four instances per GPU. Each type description is omitted independently with probability 0.3. We evaluate every 500 updates on validation data from the training sources, using up to 1,000 instances per source. We retain the checkpoint with the highest mean F1 across these sources and use validation loss to break ties. Loss settings. Using the same validation data, we select β = 0 and null-class weight of ω = 0.1. The latter is compared with 0.03 in shorter preliminary run. The relation null-class weight is also 0.1, and the relation loss coefficient is λ = 1. Both entity and relation decision rewards use = 8 samples, noise scale σ = 1, and coefficient ρ = 0.5. We increase ρ linearly from zero to 0.5 during the first 200 updates. Calibration settings. For the main results, we fit the entity temperature by minimising the multi-class Brier score on calibration data from the training sources. We search 57 log-spaced temperatures from 0.25 to 4. Extraction thresholds are selected to maximise F1 on grid from 0.02 to 0.98. The reported uncorrected model uses entity temperature = 1.219 and threshold τ = 0.88. Relations use = 1 and threshold τ = 0.85, fitted on REBEL with gold entities. Event triggers reuse the entity parameters, and event arguments reuse the relation parameters. Appendix reports the additional correction and refitting analysis.

sections.content: Entities. CALON has the highest average F1 on CrossNER, the other-domain group, and personal information extraction  (Table 1)  . sections.content: Golde et al. (2025) study zero-shot NER in terms of type-name similarity and training frequency. The 150 evaluated entity types, counted separately for each benchmark, are divided into thirds using their mention counts in CALONs training data  (Table 5)  . We report macro F1 over types in each group and the Spearman correlation between training frequency and per-type F1. CALON has the highest macro F1 in all three Its correlation with training frequency groups. is small, ρ = 0.04, and its largest margin is in the rarest group, with 58.8 F1 compared with GLiNER2s 50.6. The generative baselines have positive correlations from 0.10 to 0.21 under the same grouping. However, these frequencies come from CALONs training data and do not measure the baselines own training exposure. The analysis shows that CALONs gains are not confined to its most frequent type names. It does not isolate the effects of the training data and model architecture.

sections.content: We train on nested random subsets of 100K, 250K, 500K, 1M, and 2M instances and compare them with the full 3.1M-instance model. sections.title: K Training Data
sections.content: Table 12 lists training sources that use real texts and identifies whether their annotations come from humans, released LLM annotations, or our annotation pipeline. Counts refer to the training instances used in this work rather than the sizes of the original datasets. Table 13 lists the genres and domains used for synthetic generation. Each request combines one genre with one domain. The prompts in Figure 5 ask the generator to write text, define an extraction schema, annotate the text, and list additional types that do not occur. These absent types provide explicit negative supervision after annotation checking. Type distribution. Figure 4 shows type-name frequencies before training-source sampling. Human-labelled sources have fixed inventories, with 74 entity types in Few-NERD, 55 slots in MASSIVE, and between two and 162 event types in the event datasets. Pile-NER and the re-annotated REBEL texts have broader inventories with many infrequent type names. The pooled synthetic sources contain approximately 105K entity type names, 54K relation type names, and 85K event type names. These counts describe names used in the annotations and do not assume that every distinct name denotes distinct semantic category. Domains and genres. We sample 3,000 texts per training source and up to 500 per evaluation set. Texts are encoded with the all-mpnet-base-v2 checkpoint using the SentenceTransformers framework (Reimers and Gurevych, 2019) and projected into two dimensions with UMAP. Synthetic texts occupy broader range of regions than the real-text training sources in this projection. Several evaluation including regions also contain synthetic texts, regions associated with reviews, search queries, social media, and personal information. Figure 7 shows how these regions relate to the assigned domains and genres. This is qualitative view of the sampled embeddings. Overlap in the projection does not establish equivalent data distributions or explain the performance gains on its own. Figure 3: Average micro F1 as training data increase. Solid lines use type descriptions, dashed lines use type names alone, and dotted lines show GLiNER2 with descriptions. Averages cover the 15 NER, 18 RE with gold entities, and 7 EE with gold triggers benchmarks. contained in larger ones. Architecture, objective, batch size, and checkpoint selection follow the full model. Training updates scale with dataset size, from 1,282 for 100K instances to 40,000 for the full data, so each run makes approximately the same number of passes over its data. Evaluation intervals are also scaled to give 80 evaluations per run. Each model is trained with one seed. Figure 3 reports average NER F1, RE F1 with gold entities, and event-argument F1 with gold triggers. With descriptions, entity and relation averages improve by approximately five and eight points from 100K to 500K instances. Gains after 500K are smaller and not monotonic. Event-argument F1 changes less across the smaller subsets and improves by about two points with the full data. Results with type names alone show similar pattern. Since training updates increase with dataset size, the experiment varies data and training compute together. The single-seed results do not establish whether the smaller differences are statistically reliable.

Each request combines one genre with one domain and asks the generator to produce text and an extraction schema. 23 Prompt Template (Entities). Write one realistic {genre} from the domain of {domain}, about {length} words long, in English. Make it specific and natural, with concrete names, places, numbers and dates where the genre calls for them. Then design an entity-extraction schema for this text: 6 to 12 entity types user working in {domain} would want to extract from texts like it. Include at least two pairs of closely related types that must be told apart (for example general type and more specific one, or two similar roles). Give every type one-sentence definition that would apply to other texts too. Annotate every mention of every schema type exactly as it appears in the text; schema types that do not occur get no entries. Finally list 3 to 5 further entity types that are relevant to {domain} but do not occur anywhere in this text, each with one-sentence definition. Return JSON only: {"text": "...", "types": {"type name": "definition"}, "entities": [{"text": "...", "type": "..."}], "absent_types": {"type name": "definition"}} Prompt Template (Relations). Write one realistic {genre} from the domain of {domain}, about {length} words long, in English. Make it specific and natural, with concrete names, places, organisations, products, numbers and dates where the genre calls for them, and with several entities that are related to each other. Then design an extraction schema for this text: - 6 to 12 entity types user working in {domain} would want to extract, each with one-sentence definition that would apply to other texts too; - 5 to 10 directed relation types between those entities (from head entity to tail entity), each with one-sentence definition. Include at least two pairs of closely related relation types that must be told apart (for example founded and employed by, or relation and its reverse direction). Annotate every mention of every entity type exactly as it appears in the text, and every relation of schema type that the text states between two of those mentions (head and tail copied exactly as they appear). Schema types that do not occur get no entries. Finally list 3 to 5 further relation types that would be plausible between these entities but are not stated in the text, each with one-sentence definition. Return JSON only: {"text": "...", "entity_types": {"type": "definition"}, "entities": [{"text": "...", "type": "..."}], "relation_types": {"relation": "definition"}, "relations": [{"head": "...", "relation": "...", "tail": "..."}], "absent_relations": {"relation": "definition"}} Prompt Template (Events). Write one realistic {genre} from the domain of {domain}, about {length} words long, in English. Make it specific and natural, with concrete names, places, numbers and dates where the genre calls for them, and let it report several events (things that happen or are done), with their participants, times, places and other details. Then design an event schema for this text: 3 to 6 event types user working in {domain} would want to extract, each with one-sentence definition that would apply to other texts too, and for each event type 2 to 6 argument roles (the participants and attributes of such an event), each with one-sentence definition. Include at least one pair of closely related event types that must be told apart. Annotate every event of every schema type in the text: its type, its trigger (the single word, occasionally short phrase, that most directly expresses the event, copied exactly) and its arguments (role and the span filling it, copied exactly as it appears; only roles of that event type). Event types of the schema that do not occur get no events. Finally list 2 to 4 further event types that are relevant to {domain} but do not occur anywhere in this text, each with one-sentence definition.
